question: Implement a useIntersectionObserver custom React hook that tracks whether an element enters the viewport. Support threshold and rootMargin options, clean up the observer on unmount, and demonstrate lazy-loading images and infinite scroll with it.
expectedPoints: Uses useEffect with cleanup to disconnect the observer on unmount.
Handles null/undefined ref by checking targetRef.current and resetting state.
Uses a ref to store the latest options to avoid re-observing on every render.
Returns both entry and isIntersecting for flexibility.
Supports threshold, rootMargin, root, and triggerOnce options.
followUps: How would you modify the hook to support a custom root element (e.g., a scrollable container)?
What if the options change frequently? How would you handle that without creating a new observer each time?
How would you implement a version that returns the intersection ratio instead of just a boolean?
childExplanation: Imagine you're reading a long article and want to load images only when they come into view, like turning on a light only when you enter a room. The IntersectionObserver API lets us detect when an element becomes visible, and this custom hook wraps that logic so we can easily reuse it in any component.
detailedExplanation:
Problem Statement & Constraints

Implement a custom React hook useIntersectionObserver that tracks whether a DOM element enters the viewport (or a specified root element). The hook must:

  • Accept a ref to the target element (or return one).
  • Support options: threshold (number or array of numbers) and rootMargin (string).
  • Return an entry object (the latest IntersectionObserverEntry) or a boolean isIntersecting.
  • Clean up the observer on unmount or when the ref changes.
  • Handle edge cases: null ref, ref changes, options changes.

Performance constraints: The observer should be created only when needed and properly disconnected. No memory leaks.

Naive / Baseline Solution

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function useIntersectionObserver(ref, options = {}) {
  const [isIntersecting, setIsIntersecting] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!ref.current) return;
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
      setIsIntersecting(entry.isIntersecting);
    }, options);
    observer.observe(ref.current);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [ref, options]);

  return isIntersecting;
}

Time complexity: O(1) per observation. Space complexity: O(1) for the observer. This naive version works but has issues: it doesn't handle ref changes correctly (the effect depends on the ref object, which may not change when the ref's current changes), and it doesn't return the full entry object. Also, options are compared by reference, causing unnecessary re-observations.

Production Implementation

import { useEffect, useState, useRef } from 'react';

interface UseIntersectionObserverOptions {
  threshold?: number | number[];
  rootMargin?: string;
  root?: Element | Document | null;
  triggerOnce?: boolean;
}

interface UseIntersectionObserverReturn {
  entry: IntersectionObserverEntry | null;
  isIntersecting: boolean;
}

function useIntersectionObserver(
  targetRef: React.RefObject<Element>,
  options: UseIntersectionObserverOptions = {}
): UseIntersectionObserverReturn {
  const [entry, setEntry] = useState<IntersectionObserverEntry | null>(null);
  const [isIntersecting, setIsIntersecting] = useState(false);
  const observerRef = useRef<IntersectionObserver | null>(null);
  const optionsRef = useRef(options);
  optionsRef.current = options; // always keep latest options

  useEffect(() => {
    const element = targetRef.current;
    if (!element) {
      // No element to observe, reset state
      setEntry(null);
      setIsIntersecting(false);
      return;
    }

    // Clean up previous observer if any
    if (observerRef.current) {
      observerRef.current.disconnect();
    }

    const { threshold, rootMargin, root, triggerOnce } = optionsRef.current;

    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      ([latestEntry]) => {
        setEntry(latestEntry);
        setIsIntersecting(latestEntry.isIntersecting);
        if (triggerOnce && latestEntry.isIntersecting) {
          observer.unobserve(element);
        }
      },
      { threshold, rootMargin, root }
    );

    observer.observe(element);
    observerRef.current = observer;

    return () => {
      observer.disconnect();
      observerRef.current = null;
    };
  }, [targetRef.current]); // only re-run when the actual DOM element changes

  return { entry, isIntersecting };
}

Time complexity: O(1) per observation. Space complexity: O(1) for the observer and state. Design decisions:

  • Using optionsRef to always read the latest options without causing re-observations on every options change. This avoids unnecessary observer creation.
  • Dependency on targetRef.current ensures the effect re-runs only when the actual element changes, not when the ref object identity changes.
  • Returning both entry and isIntersecting gives flexibility: consumers can use the boolean for simple visibility checks or the full entry for more advanced use cases (e.g., intersection ratio).
  • triggerOnce option: when true, the observer stops observing after the first intersection, useful for lazy-loading images.

Edge Cases & Gotchas

  • Null ref: If targetRef.current is null (e.g., before mount), the effect returns early and resets state.
  • Ref changes: When the element changes (e.g., conditional rendering), the effect cleans up the old observer and creates a new one for the new element.
  • Options changes: The hook does not re-observe when options change (by design). To force re-observation, the consumer can use a key prop to remount the component.
  • Multiple thresholds: The threshold can be an array; the callback fires for each threshold crossing. The hook handles this correctly by storing the latest entry.
  • Root margin: rootMargin string like "10px 0px 0px 0px" works as expected.

Real-World Usage

// Lazy-loading images
function LazyImage({ src, alt }) {
  const imgRef = useRef(null);
  const { isIntersecting } = useIntersectionObserver(imgRef, { triggerOnce: true });

  return (
    <img
      ref={imgRef}
      src={isIntersecting ? src : ''}
      alt={alt}
      style={{ minHeight: 200 }}
    />
  );
}

// Infinite scroll
function InfiniteList() {
  const sentinelRef = useRef(null);
  const { isIntersecting } = useIntersectionObserver(sentinelRef, {
    rootMargin: '200px',
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (isIntersecting) {
      loadMoreItems();
    }
  }, [isIntersecting]);

  return (
    <div>
      <!-- list items -->
      <div ref={sentinelRef} style={{ height: 1 }} />
    </div>
  );
}
⚠ Common Interview Pitfall

Many candidates forget to handle the case where the ref's current element changes after the initial mount. They put the ref object itself in the dependency array, which doesn't trigger the effect when the element changes (since the ref object identity stays the same). Always use targetRef.current in the dependency array.

Senior signal: The use of a ref to store the latest options (optionsRef) is a pattern to avoid unnecessary observer re-creation. However, be aware that if the consumer changes options that affect the observer's behavior (like rootMargin), the observer won't pick up the change until the element changes. In production, you might want to add a separate effect that disconnects and reconnects the observer when options change, but that can lead to flickering. A more robust approach is to use a key prop to force remount.
